description: 2.7 billion people still have no access to the Internet. In a world that is ever more digital, being offline has become a new form of exclusion.

hero.hook: Kenya invented payment by phone ten years before Europe, because it had almost no bank branches.

blocks.text: While rich societies live through a revolution driven by artificial intelligence, a brutal fact remains: **2.7 billion people**, about one third of humanity, still have no access to the Internet.

This **digital divide** is not just a technical lag. It has become a real barrier that keeps millions of people away from education, health care and the world economy. Here is why it persists, and how some countries are trying to close it.

In 2024, about 5.4 billion people were connected to the Internet worldwide, but growth has stalled in the poorest regions. Europe and North America are above 90% coverage, while sub-Saharan Africa sits at only 37%.

This exclusion has several causes. First, missing infrastructure: operators judge fiber optic cable too expensive to lay in some remote regions. Then price: in certain countries, a basic entry-level [[smartphone]] costs several months of wages. Finally, language (about 70% of web content is in English) and the lack of digital training limit use even where a connection exists.

sections.title: A world map running at two speeds

blocks.text: The divide acts as a multiplier of inequality. In a world where remote work, online shopping and online learning on [[MOOC]] platforms are becoming the norm, being unconnected means becoming invisible to the world economy.

blocks.caption: In many rural regions, a mobile phone is the only way online

blocks.text: Kenya shows another path. With too few bank branches, the country adopted a payment system based on plain text messages as early as 2007: [[Kenyan M-Pesa]], ten years ahead of Europe. It let millions of people with no bank account make secure transactions from an ordinary phone.
Kenya nicknamed this strategy technological “leapfrogging”: rather than build expensive, outdated infrastructure, the country jumped straight to a cheaper and more modern solution.

To reach the most isolated villages, new players are betting on space. The [[Starlink]] project puts thousands of satellites into low orbit, which brings fast connections to deserts and high mountains without laying a single cable.

But the subscription and the hardware are still priced for Western customers, which puts these solutions out of reach for the poorest rural populations without outside help. Technology alone will therefore not close the digital divide: it also takes political will to treat Internet access as a public good.

sections.title: Satellite Internet, a solution with conditions

blocks.text: The fast rise of artificial intelligence threatens to widen the gap further. It demands enormous computing power and enormous amounts of data, resources held by a handful of countries and companies. Unconnected populations then risk depending on tools designed without regard for their culture or their language.

The skills gap between connected and unconnected pupils could also open very quickly. The task of the coming years is no longer only to deliver a connection, but to guarantee fair access to the creation of digital value, by combining lower costs, local content and training.

2.7 billion people are still shut out of the Internet, and artificial intelligence risks making that divide worse. Closing it means turning connectivity into a genuine public good, not just a product for sale.

subtitle: One third of humanity offline
title: The global digital divide
